Jeremy Schon & Greg Ormont

Jeremy Schon and Greg Ormont are guitarists, songwriters, and founding members of Pigeons Playing Ping Pong. This constantly touring band attracts its “flock,” a multi-generational group of music lovers who appreciate the Pigeons’ balance of musicianship and improvisation infused with humor.
Jeremy and Greg were interviewed via Zoom on March 8, 2024 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m very pleased, at 10 AM in the morning, to have Greg Ormont and Jeremy Schon here from the band Pigeons Playing Ping Pong. Welcome, gentlemen.
Thanks for having us.
Yeah, this is just like — I have to say, I don’t know how many families around the country can say this, but you have three generations of fans in our family.
Oh wow.
My daughter and her family, our grandkids, are all members of your flock.
And therefore you’re the honorary grandfather in the flock?
The honorary flock grandfather I guess.
The grandflocker?
Yeah.
There you go, you’re the first — you know there might be other grandfather fans but you’re officially deemed the grandflocker.
You know I sense that there might be a song there.
Yeah. You know we have an hour, right? It could be done. That’s easy.
Do you fellows get song inspiration from unexpected places?

Most of our songs are written from Zoom interviews so no, it’s pretty consistent here. But it is funny how like that little phrase like, you know I think there’s a song there with a funny little joke, that’s actually one of our more known tunes over the past fifteen years as a band is a song called F-U, that the chorus goes F-U-N-K, spelling funk. But that was — I’m telling you it was generated exactly how we just discussed grandflocker, like it was just one of those quick things that ended up, we took it and ran with it. I think we had our guitars in our hands, that’s the only difference. So it could come from that or it can be, you know, sitting down and practicing, coming up with ideas as a group, as individuals. You’ve just got to be a sponge as a musician, right?
So you have your guitar in your hand and you’ve got this little phrase, where do your hands first go, Jeremy? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

You know? Where do they go? I guess they go to B minor — yeah — they go in so many different directions, it depends on the mood you know. Well like F-U is like all right, this is funk, this has clearly got to be a funk song so I mean I went to like a Dorian minor groove you know? Now it’s like easy to go to Afro-beats. You know. I’ll put this down.
That’s cool. And you used the word I was going to ask you, were you both at University of Maryland?
Um hum.
We both graduated in the class of 2010.
And I noticed they had — I went to their website, they had three jazz ensembles. And I wonder if you were involved in that scene?

No. I mean we enjoyed that scene thoroughly. And you know we took one jazz class when we were in college, which the subject matter was amazing for. But no, I mean I was a marketing and information systems major and Greg was a communications major. We just loved playing music and you know it’s always been a passion project for us.
Was it hard for the band to get like rehearsal space on campus being that you weren’t music majors?

Well I’ll tell you if we did try to get rehearsal space on campus it probably would have been very tough. But we always found someone’s basement or garage, which was also tough. And you know we changed locations a lot because people would get noise complaints and then we’d have to move on, like, “All right well I guess we can’t practice in Sam’s garage anymore.”

Did the group evolve from a cover band? Most bands when they start rehearsing they may have a goal to like, “Let’s play some gigs.” So in order to play gigs you have to play what people want to hear I guess. And did you evolve from playing covers to then inserting your own original material? Greg do you want to field that question?

Sure. Yeah I mean we did start playing covers early on. We did, from the beginning we always did our own spin on covers and, you know, we started as an acoustic duo and would mash-up two songs into one or change the genre of the cover we’re playing. But yeah I mean we did want to, you know after meeting in the dorm rooms and playing we did want to play out. We wanted to play in front of people and when you don’t have a lot of material you can certainly play others to get the ball rolling and get the cobwebs off and get the momentum of playing live under your fingers. And we did start with covers but very quickly inserted our originals. It was almost like a band-aid until we had enough to garner a full set.

Yeah. It was definitely a mix. And also it’s just really fun playing songs that you love you know. We’ve always enjoyed having the chance to play some of our favorite songs. And like it really started off as just a jamming in the dorm room to like oh let’s play this © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

song that we both really enjoy, and then we were playing it for ten people at the coffee shop. And now we probably don’t play that song anymore but maybe we play a different cover song that we all love as a band you know. The whole premise is still the same, you know we’re having a lot of fun playing music it’s just that more people show up now.
A lot more. If you’re riding in a — do you ride in a van or a bus usually on your tours?

It really depends on the weekend and the run you know. If it’s an extended tour where we’re out for at least like four nights to three weeks then we can sometimes take a tour bus. But otherwise we’ll tour in a Chevy 15-passenger van and trailer.

I remember those days, and I wonder, there’s a term in music of course called paying dues. And did you guys go through those five-in-a-motel and you know, taking as many crackers from the restaurant as you could to get through this particular series of gigs?

Early on five-in-a-motel sounds great. Because we were on people’s floors you know. After each show in our first few years we would go out in the crowd and make friends, ‘cause (A) we’re social people and (B) we needed a place to stay. So we would meet people, chat, find out what their situation was and then meet up as a band it’s like, “Okay I found someone with two couches but they have to wake up early.” Or “I found, you know a pull out bed but they’re having an after-party so it might be hard to sleep. So there was, I think one of the lower points, while I really look at it like romantically like I think this is part of the process, but I woke up next to cat litter one morning after playing a gig, it’s like what people think we do and what we actually do, right? Now we’re fortunate that, you know sometimes we have a tour bus or we definitely have a bed to sleep in, and dues were paid but, if I could recommend paying your dues in your early twenties that’s probably for the best. Mid-thirties would be a little tougher but you know for the love of the music I’d wake up next to kitty litter again.
Oh that is a great quote that we’re going to have to use down the road.
You got your quote? Perfect. Headline.

I know exactly what you’re saying because I was in this business when I was in my thirties and I thought why am I doing this now, it should have been like ten years ago, earlier. Did you have a sense of what it meant to “make it” in the business? Did you have goals, those nights you were sleeping on couches and you’re thinking about where are we trying to go with this?

I mean yes and no. I mean first like you know we were really, we were just having a great time just traveling around the country playing music for people, meeting new people everywhere we went. And we were just like hey, how can we, let’s keep riding this. You know let’s see where this takes us you know. But you know when we started the band you know there was no like, oh we’re going to start this band and we’re going to play in this band for thirty years. Like 16 years later it’s amazing and such a gift that we’re still a © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
band and you know who could have like seen that happening when we were in the College Park dorms like 16 years ago.
Yeah you’ve been together longer than The Beatles. Maybe you should go for the Rolling Stones you know, break their record.
I’m down.
Yeah. We started early enough.

Yeah. When you get — I’m wondering if there’s ever been a tune that you’re working on, and you’ve got this great groove going, a set of chords, and maybe you have a vocal but aah, it’s just not working. And have you ever had the circumstance where you just make it an instrumental?

I don’t know if we’ve ever gone, made a vocal tune instrumental, but we’ve definitely taken instrumental tunes and added vocals. I mean we’ve definitely, we’ve had tons of songs that like you know we’ll play as a group in rehearsal and sometimes it don’t gel or sometimes it’s like aah, this doesn’t feel right. And sometimes they’ll kind of get put on the shelf. But I’m not sure if we’ve ever taken a vocal tune and turned it instrumental. But I like the idea.

Well when I listen to the song “Horizon” which you’ve been doing what for ten years now, it’s got that beautiful vamp in the beginning with those two guitar lines and it lasts a long time. And you’re not really — this of course is just my opinion — you’re not really jamming, you’re playing this thing for 32 bars or whatever, and when you recorded that did you feel like it doesn’t need anything more than that, we’re just going to do that for quite some time and then we’re going to add something on top of it and do that for another 16 bars. I’m just trying to get into your head how that worked.

You’ve cracked the code. I mean we’ve, as a band you know and as individual people, we’ve always, I mean we all listen to a lot of instrumental music, especially like kind of groove-oriented instrumental music you know like people like John Scofield more in the jazz world. And like we love to be able to vamp on a cool groove. If there’s anything that, you know, for “Horizon” I feel like we thought all right, the simple guitar melody that’s happening is very simple, but it catchy enough. And I don’t know, somehow we felt that we didn’t need full-on vocals you know. And yeah. But we love to ride a vamp you know.

And in those instances you know, like Jeremy wrote the bulk of that song and when he does he’ll send them my way usually or I’ll be sitting next to him in college or whatever the time period is. And I’ll think about adding vocals, almost always, where we sing often. We have a lot of instrumentals but the majority have vocals. And the intro I ended up, you know coming across this like idea, and the song kind of harkened me back to some other concerts I’ve been to where there’s a vamp that’s building and you kind of © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

soak in the bliss of it. You soak in the patience of it and just kind of be there in the moment, and you know it’s kind of the preparation before the build. You know? And intro vocals talk about this, like I walk into the show, I finally hang my coat, you know, find my seating and enjoy the show. And then the song basically starts and I thought it was so like peaceful and warm and happy that it can live on its own and after the entire journey of the song where it goes from happy and peaceful to like has the minor, you know solo section, the jam section that adds a lot of tension, builds, builds, builds with anticipation, and then finally crashes into a triumphant chord progression. That to me was like okay if the intro is me walking into the show, the instrumental section is the concert, and as I walk out feeling happier than I did when I came in all I could say is celebrate the people you love, which is the anthem at the end of the song. So for me like that was kind of a conceptual thing where, you know, it kind of encapsulated a night out at a fun concert where — oh that’s my cat Emmy — all you can say is like I got there, the music overtook me, and at the end just celebrate the people you love. You know? It was kind of a conceptual decision to withhold the vocals in the middle.
Oh it’s Beethovenesque.
That’s another first.
Beethoven used the same four chords.
Yeah if Beethoven used four chords, you heard it here with Monk the Grandflocker.

Well the extended section sitting like that and they make the changes that much more effective, when they finally get there, of course you’re building the volume and the bass and drummer adding their thing. I guess I’m just, I admire it but I’ve noticed, Jeremy, the same, a similar thing about your soloing. I can imagine a music theory class where the professor might say, “Notice how Mr. Schon used motivic development and thematic inflection in his solos” because they just seem really well thought out and not random.

Thank you, first of all, appreciate that. I take that as a compliment. You know usually I mean they’re 80 percent improv you know. There’s some songs that I will write a solo for and actually play that solo. But you know when we’re improvising you know we try hard to like give people something they can kind of latch on to so I think motifs are really important in that way. And it allows us to kind of use some repetition and be patient to let it build gradually you know, versus quickly soar right to the top.
Did you ever do any comparison to the length of the particular songs on your LPs and compare them to what you do live with the same song?

Oh they’re pretty different. You know the studio, we want people, when people are at a concert, they’re in the moment you know. There’s the light show, there’s everyone around them, there’s a huge energy in the room. And, you know similarly, like Greg was saying about “Horizon,” we want people to ride that wave and let it build patiently you © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

know, and stretch it out as long as we see fitting in that exact moment. You know it’s a whole experience live. But in the studio package people are listening in their cars or sitting at home and they might not have the patience. They either listen to the 15 minute version of said song. So sometimes the five minute version will be what people listen to at home but then they get to come to the show and experience us stretching it out and taking it for a ride.

Are there things you do in the studio to try to capture that live excitement? Can you actually — do you record all four of you at the same time? And can you see each other in that kind of set up in the studio?

Yeah we record all, I mean we start off every album we’ve ever recorded we record in a big live room, usually at Wright Way Studios in Baltimore, where we have drums set up on one side and we’re all set up on the other side. Everyone’s kind of in a circle, similar to how we set up for band practice. And yeah, we just give it our all, you know, try to capture as much energy in each take while also trying to make it the perfect take. And you know we try to incorporate as much into our studio material as possible, whether it be guests, like some cool overdubs, a lot of guitar harmony over here, just to spice it up, just to give it that extra little edge that sets it apart from what we do with it live. Just ‘cause we can’t encapsulate the full energy of a thousand people in a room, a light show, and that fan band energy interchange in the studio. Like, it’s not really possible. So we try to put as much else that we can think of into our studio recordings to give them that extra boost.
Well Greg, when you do your vocals in the studio to you sing while you’re playing or do you do it after the fact?

No, I am afforded the luxury of not having to play two instruments at once with singing and playing, so I’m able to really focus on the vocals and conversely I’m able to really focus on my guitar playing when we’re laying down the foundation of the songs together because I don’t sing during those group sessions. It’s more so about the instrumentation and the drumming when we play the initial track together. Afterward, once we’ve worked on the individual parts I come into the studio and just sing, which is really like, it’s a luxury, it truly feels like, because I don’t have to split my attention so I can be more, I hope accurate and more thoughtful with each piece of what I contribute to the band when I’m recording, which is really nice. The interesting thing is vocally I have no issue like focusing and executing what I need to do. Sometimes it’s hard to play the guitar without singing due to muscle memory, you know, so before we go into the studio I’ll often practice, as well as practice for the other guys to get through the structure of the song without my voice leading the changes, whether it’s verse to chorus or verse to pre-chorus, or this one’s a half chorus, this one’s a full chorus. If I’m not singing the melodies it’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

funny, like even if we play the song fifty times this is like maybe the first or third time we’ve ever done it where I’m not singing. So it’s worthwhile to practice that as well, which we do, and even for my own sake, just to — you know I’ve found that certain sections it helps for me to even mouth how I sing to get my right hand to do what it normally does when I’m playing and singing.
Yeah you’ve got this thing down and —
Exactly.
If you don’t do it it’s weird.

Exactly. It’s one way. It’s absolutely that you know. It’s funny. But it’s a fun challenge and we love recording for that reason particularly is like we can really focus on — you know when I’m on stage I love to perform and rock out and connect with the crowd and look at the crowd and not my fingers if you don’t need to and jump up and down. And with the excitement of jumping up and down comes a real focus on not pulling your strings and falling slightly out of tune. So it’s nice to not have that going on as well and I could just sit and really focus at getting my fingers dead on the fret board you know, keeping the proper strings muted and execute more technically.
“Keeping the proper strings muted.” That reminds me of Bucky Pizzarelli telking about Freddie Green and the way he strummed, and that a lot of his strumming was only two or three strings.
Yeah.

Yeah. It’s a little aside but regarding strumming and playing rhythm I noticed that you often times have — I don’t know if it’s a phase shifter or some kind of effect on your guitar that really I think is distinctive with the Pigeons. It gives you a band sound.

Well thank you for saying that, that’s definitely one of the hardest things to do, right, is to sound like yourself whether as a guitarist or as a band, and like you said a lot of bands start with covers and inspiration but it’s hard to find your voice. I think one of the biggest things that the band has worked on over the past decade plus is honing in our sound and filling space without a keyboardist or a percussionist per se. So most instrumentation includes keyboards and the fact that we don’t have that has really informed my playing because where a keyboard would fill in gaps and, you know, lay down textural pads, that falls more so on my territory. I mean we all take turns but it’s kind of forced me to learn to comp and support the band and help elevate the other players by filling space, almost like as a keyboard would. So with that comes, yeah, some phasing, I use a lot of my wah pedal combined with a delay pedal and a volume sweep on the guitar itself, so you’re hearing less attack, you’re hearing less a guitarist and more so of swelling textures that — a lot of times when Jeremy is taking a solo I don’t want to sound like a guitar. We already © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
have one that’s screaming so I almost want to create some contrast for him to poke out more.
Yeah I was listening to a tune yesterday, I can’t recall the name but it was near the beginning I said, “Oh there’s a Wurlitzer electric piano in there.” And it was you. So it definitely works.

Maybe. And for what it’s worth I mean in the studio it’s another opportunity where we can afford to have maybe some background keys or add a percussionist, or maybe add a horn section here where we don’t have the opportunity to do that live every show. So it’s another opportunity to, you know, fill sonic space, to try something new, to collaborate with phenomenal musicians, and elevate the track for the studio setting. And then when that happens live when we have a guest on stage it’s like adding a new spice to a stew, like it’s what is this, this is bright, this is exciting, not just for us but hopefully for the crowd as well.
Do you depend on outside ears when you’re doing a recording, especially in the mixing? Do you have a producer or do you just sort of do it yourself?

So we work, we’ve been working with this guy Steve Wright at Wright Way Studios for probably ten years now. And I mean you know he runs the studio, he’s like the lead engineer there. And he’s got an amazing ear. He’ll tell us instantly after taping like, “Oh you were just barely out of tune, do it again.” We spend a lot of time tuning. But he will give us as much feedback as we kind of ask for you know. Often times we’ll be like, “Hey we’re torn between these two songs. Which one do you think would fit this group of songs for a record more?” And he’ll give us feedback and you know sometimes we’ll be like, “You’re right” and you know it helps be a tiebreaker, you know sometimes when the band is just torn and we just like can’t make a decision on our own we’ll call in Steve and be like, “Hey, what do you think we should do?” And often times we’ll ask other musicians just for feedback if we’re just like stuck in a spot or just really indecisive you know. But we’ve never worked with like a true like producer, someone who kind of gets in there, works on the songs with us before, and the whole pre-production to the studio to the thing. We haven’t done that yet. Maybe one day we will but as far as we’re concerned Steve is our producer and he does an amazing job. He’s incredibly patient —
Are you all in the booth when things are mixed?

Sometimes. More or less though he’ll mix like after a session or he’ll mix months or weeks after a session and he’ll just send us a Dropbox link with a bunch of mixes and we’ll sometimes get together or sometimes just individually send notes. But often times we will go in for a mix or added sessions and it’s really fun. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
I remember the days when, you know the band would all be in the booth and people are asking, “Okay which fader is mine?” so that they could come up and like — everybody wanted more of themselves.
That’s when the engineer creates some dummy faders on the side.
The dummy fader.
You could have all three of these.
Okay name this Pigeon song [scats] Obviously I didn’t sing it very well.
[scats]
It’s an instrumental guitar riff. Okay time’s up. Well I was trying to sing “Havana.”
“Havana!” You know I was about to say “Havana” but I wasn’t a hundred percent sure.
Oh okay.
I really was.

Yeah if I look at my notes here you know I have this motif thing down I wrote. And that is I think a great example of this lick that rhythmically repeats itself many times but you’ve got these little changes in there. Where did that come from?
That was one of my favorite ones when I was writing it. Like that really — because it was very interesting. It’s in a harmonic major key, which is a bit strange.
Can you explain that?

So it’s in the key of G major. I’m 90 percent sure. I’ve got to think of my guitar. [plays guitar] I don’t know, something like that. But it’s kind of like an interesting line. It largely wraps over a G major 7. That’s like at its center. But then there’s a bunch of chords that kind of wrap around this riff that do not really lie in the traditional key of G major. Right. Okay yes, so it’s in G harmonic major, which is I believe a G major scale — what is it, a flat six.
Oh there’s an E flat in there. Yeah.

Yeah. So it leaves us with a 4 minor chord and also that flat six major seventh. Actually well I guess technically that would be — it should be augmented I guess. But I wasn’t thinking of this stuff when I wrote it actually.
It’s after the fact usually.
What?
It’s after the fact usually — ooh look what I did there.

A guitar student asked me about it and I realized I didn’t really know what key it was in. I just, you know it’s often better to not think too deeply about the key signature when you’re writing because you don’t want to limit yourself. Like a lot of earlier songs we wrote you know were very much diatonic, perfectly in a key. But you know when you just kind of use your ear or let your fingers just take you places you know, you’re going © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

to end up with a more interesting product in the end. I mean, usually. And now and then, that one’s pretty interesting just ‘cause it’s a strange chord progression of like G major 7 to C minor 7 to E flat major 7, D 7. It’s really, it’s kind of, it’s almost got like a Middle Eastern vibe to it, but I don’t know it’s just different.

There’s a tune that I can’t remember the name of, which I think I ended up trying to vocalize here and it’s a very Cuban-sounding thing [scats] like it’s not a rumba but it’s some kind of dance. And it was reminiscent of that but it’s really a great tune so,
Thanks.
Keep playing it.

No I love playing that. I mean that song, it’s fun to play and it was actually also challenging, you know I had to practice that a lot to not like blow it live. But yeah, that’s a really fun song you know.

You seem to be, the whole band seems to be pretty spontaneous on stage and in watching the videos and actually my daughter mentioned this, watching you live, trying to see what cues are you all giving each other when you’re vamping on something, sometimes it’s musically apparent that it’s building and building and needs — it feels like a change now, but other times I’m just wondering do you have eye contact, body language that moves you from one section to another? Greg, what do you think?

Well I think, like you said a lot of times the music will dictate a need for a change. It depends on if we’re in a true freeform section or if we know where the — like no matter what even if it’s freeform unless we’ve decided to play a one song set and truly improvise for 75 minutes, generally speaking we know where the destination is but there are multiple ways of getting there and a lot of times it’s as simple as if we feel as though we’ve taken this route, we’ve built tension and it’s time to release, it’s as simple as looking at each other, looking at each other before the one, kind of just being like yup, just a short little nod or even eye contact. And then over time, because we know where the destination is depending on how improvisational the moment is, I could look over at one of the guys and they don’t even have to look, they just nod looking forward, and I’m like okay he sees that I’m looking over at him, we’re ready to proceed to the next section. When we’re in true, true improvisational moments we do have hand signals or body language signals that can be utilized to refer to a chord in the key that we could go to but that is much less common than kind of, I mean we’ve been playing together for — we’ve put in the 10,000 hours as a group let alone as individuals, and we know each other’s tendencies. We’ve also learned the hard way that like if there’s a sense that one out of the four of us isn’t ready to move on, don’t move on. You know? ‘Cause there’s a patience there where even if we have to vamp for another 8 or 16 or 32 we’d all rather go together than you know jump the gun prematurely. So, and fortunately our fans afford us that © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
luxury. They’re there for the ride. You know they’re not going to be — “Hey you know the form is off guys.”
That’s when it’s like, “Come on fellas.”
Yeah. Enough of this vamp, right? No. So we’re patient, we’re conservative, and we really keep open ears across the board, whether feeding each other motifs or progressing the structure along.

Yeah. A lot of changes will happen like live with just like, you know, someone will introduce a new chord, you know, Greg will start playing like a D over the A minor that Ben is rolling you know. And then we all hear him and we’re like all right, let’s follow that. You know. And or Ben could often times introduce a progression when we land into like, oh if we’re in a one-chord jam like Ben could suddenly introduce a chord progression on the bass you know, usually revolving around some chord tones to keep it safe at least initially, but you know really it’s whatever goes live and we all really have to have open ears at every moment, otherwise we might miss either an audio, a musical cue or a visual cue.
Do you ever break into a swing groove?

Sure. Absolutely. Yeah. We talk about swing and how swung it should be all the time. You know our drummer, we all afford each other a lot of leeway to take it wherever it may be and that’s not just how Jeremy described our musical progressions but if the drummer wants to try a new beat like we all just feel it. And I think a large portion of that is, you know the understanding that we have that freedom and leeway, and also a lack of ego for individuals because if someone makes a decision that is pretty finite, like switching a groove, there is no forcing the group back to where it was from us. There’s all right, we’re taking this turn, one of us took a leap and we’re jumping with him. You know like there’s no creative struggle when we’re improvising. I just think that’s so important you know. It’s something you learn over time. Like I hear this idea, I totally hear this modulating, and if it’s not felt musically or just visually you can sense that the guys aren’t ready to move on, if you force it, boy is that not going to work out. You know? So it’s really important to be constantly thinking about the group. We’re one of four people. That’s the minority you know? The group needs to decide where the music goes, not you.

Well said. There was an interesting moment from a video that you were playing on a New Year’s Eve and you were playing “Auld Lang Syne.” I think you were waiting for the balloons to fall or something, and they weren’t.

Which year? That happens every year, Monk. We’re cursed with New Year’s balloons. Actually this year though I think the curse didn’t rear it’s head but man there’s been multiple, multiple times that the balloons haven’t dropped, the string breaks and now how © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

do you even get the balloons to drop? There was one concert when we were playing a slightly smaller venue, still like a thousand people but not as, like the way that it was set up the string that you used to pull the balloon net were within the crowd and I don’t know if the security fell asleep or took a coffee break but a fan pulled it at around 11:40 PM.
